parts.title: Part 2
parts.context: A guide shows visitors around a chocolate factory.
script: Welcome to Hollow Hill Chocolate. My name's Tom, and I'll be showing you around the factory today.
The company was started in 1962 by two sisters, Margaret and Ellen Hill, who began by making chocolates in their kitchen and selling them at the local market.
Most of our cocoa beans come from Ghana, where we work directly with farming cooperatives. We also buy a small amount from Ecuador for our special dark bars.
You're welcome to take photos throughout the tour, except in the packing area, where some of our machines were specially designed for us and the designs are confidential.
People often ask which product is most popular. Milk chocolate used to be our best seller, but for the past three years it's been our dark chocolate with sea salt.
And at the end of the tour, everyone will receive a free bar to take home. The gift shop is optional.
Let me explain the process as we go. In the roasting room, the beans are heated to bring out their flavour.
Next, in the grinding room, the shells are removed, and the inside of the bean, called the nib, is ground into a thick paste.
After that comes conching, where the mixture is stirred continuously for many hours to make it smooth.
Then the chocolate goes through tempering, where it's carefully cooled and reheated to precise temperatures, which gives it a shiny surface.
Finally, in moulding, the chocolate is poured into shapes and left to set. Wrapping, by the way, is done entirely by machine.

parts.context: Two history students, Sofia and Owen, discuss their project on a local textile mill.
script: Sofia, why did you want to do our project on the old mill?
Partly because my great-grandmother worked there. I grew up hearing stories about it.
That's a great connection. What's been the most useful source so far?
Definitely the oral history recordings at the town museum. Former workers describe exactly what their days were like.
I had a problem with the company records. The wage books for the 1920s are incomplete, because many of them were damaged in a flood.
That's a shame. What surprised you most?
How young some of the workers were. In the 1850s, children as young as eight worked there.
Yes, that shocked me too. Now, Dr Price said we can choose the format. I'd like to do a podcast instead of an essay, using clips from the recordings.
Good idea. Let's check the main facts for the timeline. The mill opened in 1842.
At first it was powered by water from the river. Steam engines came later.
At its peak, it employed around twelve hundred workers.
And the main product was cotton towels, which were sold all over the country.
It finally closed in 1978, mainly because of cheaper imports from abroad.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.context: A lecture on the migration of monarch butterflies.
script: Today I want to talk about one of the most remarkable journeys in the natural world: the migration of the monarch butterfly.

Every autumn, millions of monarchs in North America fly south, some of them travelling up to four thousand kilometres. Most of the eastern population spends the winter in a small area of mountain forests in Mexico, where they cluster on trees in their millions.

How do they find their way, especially since none of them has made the journey before? Research shows that monarchs navigate using the sun. They have an internal clock in their antennae, which allows them to adjust for the sun's movement during the day. On cloudy days, they appear to use a magnetic compass as well.

Another fascinating feature is their lifespan. Summer monarchs live for only a few weeks. But the generation that migrates south lives up to eight months, long enough to survive the winter and begin the journey back north in spring.
Monarch caterpillars feed only on milkweed plants, which contain chemicals that make the butterflies poisonous to birds. Their bright orange colour is a warning to predators.

Unfortunately, the eastern monarch population has fallen by around eighty percent since the 1990s. A major cause is the loss of milkweed, much of which has been destroyed by the herbicides used on farms. In Mexico, illegal logging has also damaged the forests where they spend the winter.
There is some good news. Many people across North America are now helping by planting native flowers, including milkweed, in their gardens, creating stopping points along the migration route.

passages.title: The Golden Fibre
paragraphs: For more than a century, jute was among the most important crops in the Bengal delta, the region that now forms Bangladesh and the Indian state of West Bengal. Because of its golden colour and the wealth it generated, it became known as the 'golden fibre'. Jute grows best in hot, humid conditions with plenty of rain, and the delta's fertile soils, renewed by annual floods, are ideal for it.

Turning the plant into fibre is labour-intensive. After harvesting, the long stalks are tied in bundles and soaked in ponds or slow-moving rivers for two to three weeks, a process called retting. Bacteria in the water break down the soft tissue, allowing workers to strip the fibres from the stalks by hand. The fibres are then washed and dried in the sun.

Jute became a global commodity in the nineteenth century. The Scottish city of Dundee, which already had a textile industry, developed methods for spinning jute by machine, and its mills processed huge quantities of fibre imported from Bengal. Jute sacks were used around the world to transport grain, sugar, coffee and cotton. Later, mills were built in Bengal itself, and after independence, Bangladesh's Adamjee Jute Mills became the largest jute mill in the world.

From the 1970s, however, the industry went into decline. Cheap synthetic fibres, particularly polypropylene, replaced jute in many uses, and demand fell sharply. Many mills closed, including Adamjee in 2002, and thousands of workers lost their jobs.

In recent years, concern about plastic pollution has given jute a second chance. Unlike plastic, jute is biodegradable, and growing it absorbs carbon dioxide. In 2010 Bangladesh passed a law requiring certain products, including rice and sugar, to be packed in jute bags. Researchers have also developed new jute-based materials. One of the best known is the Sonali bag, a plastic-like bag made from cellulose extracted from jute, invented by the Bangladeshi scientist Mubarak Ahmad Khan.

Scientific research has also strengthened the crop's future. In 2010, a team of Bangladeshi scientists led by Maqsudul Alam decoded the jute genome, opening the way to varieties that produce better fibre or can withstand difficult conditions. Whether jute can recover its former importance remains uncertain, but its golden reputation may yet be restored.

passages.title: The Plastic We Cannot See
paragraphs: Microplastics are pieces of plastic smaller than five millimetres. Some are manufactured at this size, such as the tiny beads once added to face scrubs and toothpaste. Most, however, are produced when larger items break down, as bottles and bags are worn away by sunlight and waves. Another major source is clothing: every time synthetic fabrics such as polyester are washed, they release thousands of tiny fibres, many of which pass through water treatment plants into rivers and the sea.

Microplastics have now been found almost everywhere scientists have looked. They have been detected in snow near the summit of Mount Everest, in sediment at the bottom of the Mariana Trench, the deepest point in the ocean, and in sea ice in the Arctic. Winds and ocean currents carry them thousands of kilometres from their sources.

Inevitably, they also enter our food and drink. Shellfish such as mussels, which filter large volumes of seawater, often contain microplastics, and particles have been found in sea salt, honey and beer. A widely reported 2018 study tested bottled water from several countries and found microplastics in the great majority of samples, in many cases at higher levels than in tap water.

What this means for human health is still unclear. In 2022, researchers in the Netherlands reported finding microplastics in human blood for the first time, and particles have since been found in other parts of the body. Laboratory studies suggest that very small particles can cause inflammation in cells, but scientists do not yet know whether the levels people are exposed to cause harm.

Part of the difficulty is that microplastics are hard to measure. There are no agreed standard methods, so results from different studies are difficult to compare. Contamination is also a constant problem: plastic fibres from researchers' clothing or laboratory equipment can easily enter samples, so careful studies must include tests to check for this.

Governments have begun to act. The United States banned plastic microbeads in rinse-off cosmetics in 2015, and several other countries have followed. France has introduced a requirement for new washing machines to be fitted with filters to capture fibres. At the international level, countries have been negotiating a global treaty on plastic pollution, although agreement has proved difficult. Most experts agree that the only lasting solution is to reduce the amount of plastic produced in the first place.

passages.title: Too Many Visitors?
paragraphs: Few places illustrate the problems of mass tourism as clearly as Venice. In the 1950s, around 175,000 people lived in the city's historic centre. Today the figure is below 50,000, while the city receives tens of millions of visitors each year. On busy summer days, its narrow streets and bridges become so crowded that residents struggle to walk to work or school.

The main reason residents leave is not the crowds themselves but the cost of housing. As more apartments are converted into short-term holiday rentals, which earn owners far more than long-term lets, the supply of homes for local people shrinks and rents rise. Shops selling everyday goods close and are replaced by souvenir stalls. In my view, this transformation of homes into hotels, rather than the number of tourists alone, is the heart of the problem.

Venice has tried several measures. In 2021, after UNESCO threatened to add the city to its list of World Heritage Sites in danger, the Italian government banned large cruise ships from entering the main lagoon. In 2024, the city began charging an entry fee of five euros to day-trippers, who make up a large share of visitors but spend relatively little money in the city. The ban on cruise ships was a welcome step, but it has not solved overcrowding, since most visitors arrive by train, bus or plane. And a fee of five euros is, I believe, too small to change many people's plans.

Other cities have tried different approaches. Amsterdam has stopped approving new hotels in its centre and has limited the number of nights homes can be rented to tourists. Barcelona has announced plans to phase out holiday apartment licences, while some cities promote lesser-known neighbourhoods and nearby towns in an attempt to spread visitors more widely.

It would be wrong, however, to treat tourism simply as an enemy. In Venice and many other destinations, tourism provides a large share of jobs and income, and the money visitors spend helps to maintain historic buildings. Proposals to discourage tourism altogether would hurt many local workers.

The real question is whose interests tourism policy should serve. For too long, decisions have been shaped by what attracts the most visitors and generates the most income. I believe that the most important step is to limit the conversion of homes into short-term rentals, so that people can afford to live in their own cities. A city that loses its residents becomes little more than a theme park, and in the end that is not what visitors come to see either.

task1.text: The line graph below shows the percentage of people in four age groups who used the internet on mobile phones in one country between 2010 and 2025. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words.

chart.title: Mobile internet users by age group (%)

model: The line graph shows the proportion of people in four age groups who accessed the internet on mobile phones in one country from 2010 to 2025.

Overall, mobile internet use rose substantially in every age group. Younger people were consistently the most likely to use it, although the gap between age groups narrowed considerably over the period.

In 2010, 45% of 16 to 24-year-olds used mobile internet, compared with 30% of those aged 25 to 44. The figures for older people were much lower, at 12% for 45 to 64-year-olds and only 3% for people aged 65 and over.

Over the next fifteen years, use among the two youngest groups grew rapidly, reaching almost universal levels of 97% and 95% by 2025. The 45 to 64 age group saw an even steeper rise, from 12% to 85%. Although people aged 65 and over remained the least likely to use mobile internet, their figure increased more than twentyfold, to 62%, with the fastest growth occurring between 2015 and 2020.

task2.text: Some people believe that university education should be free for all students. To what extent do you agree or disagree? Write at least 250 words.
model: In many countries, university students pay high tuition fees and graduate with significant debts. Some people argue that higher education should instead be free for everyone. I partly agree: I believe university should be free or very low-cost for students from lower-income families, but that a completely free system for all is not the fairest use of public money.

There are strong arguments for free university education. Higher education benefits society as a whole, not only individuals, by producing the doctors, engineers and teachers a country needs. High fees may discourage talented students from poorer backgrounds from applying, which wastes ability and reinforces inequality. Countries such as Germany, where tuition is free at public universities, show that such a system can work.

However, making university free for everyone is extremely expensive, and the money must come from taxes paid by the whole population, including people who never attend university and often earn less than graduates. In practice, free systems can end up subsidising students from wealthy families, who are more likely to go to university in the first place. Funding is also limited, so some countries with free tuition restrict the number of places or have overcrowded classes.

In my view, a better approach is to target support where it is most needed. Students from low-income families should receive free tuition and grants for living costs, while those from wealthier families could pay fees, perhaps through loans that are repaid only when graduates earn above a certain income.

In conclusion, while I agree that cost should never prevent able students from going to university, I believe targeted support is fairer and more sustainable than making higher education free for all.

speaking.cue:
Describe a gift you gave to someone.
You should say:
- what the gift was
- who you gave it to

and explain how the person felt about it.
speaking.cueModel: I'd like to talk about a gift I gave my grandmother on her seventieth birthday last year. She lives in a village outside Barisal, and she's always loved gardening, but her eyesight has been getting worse, and she was finding it hard to look after her plants. So my cousins and I decided to give her something practical but personal. We bought a set of raised garden beds, which meant she wouldn't have to bend down so much, and I made a photo album to go with it. In the album, I collected old pictures of her garden over the years, along with photos of all her grandchildren helping her plant things when we were small. The raised beds were mainly my cousins' idea, but the album was mine, and it took me a few weekends to finish. When she opened it, she was quiet for a moment and then started crying, but they were happy tears. She spent the whole evening going through the pages and telling stories about each photo. I think it meant a lot to her because it showed we remembered those moments as much as she did.
